extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers (wartime public) and reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Writing short-form daily newspaper items about wartime events, combining frontline/despatch reports, official statements, human-interest sketches, and industrial/legislative news in a single edition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin items with a clear dateline/location and date (e.g., 'HEADQUARTERS, ... Nov. 6', 'Kokoda, Nov. 3').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article examples show location-first leads such as 'HEADQUARTERS, De- ...' and repeated 'Nov. 6' markers; include place and date so readers know where/when dispatches originated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Byline and source attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute pieces to the reporter or wire service (e.g., 'By OLEN W. CLEMENTS', '(AP)', 'Associated Press').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bylines for named correspondents and note wire-service origin for short dispatches. The page alternates local bylines and '(AP)' attributions indicating source and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise lead summarizing key outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with a short summary of the principal facts or results (example phrasing: 'announced the results as follows:' followed by immediate outcomes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads in these dispatches list main results up front (damaged ships, planes destroyed, message from Admiral Nimitz). Keep the lead tight and fact-forward so busy readers get the essentials immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise counts and specific factual detail
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting losses, damage, production, or personnel, give exact counts and concrete specifics (e.g., 'One heavy cruiser damaged, one transport damaged...','at least six enemy planes destroyed for each one lost').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The copy uses enumerated damage/tally lists and production figures; include numbers and measurable details rather than vague phrasing to increase credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of official statements and quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Include official messages and direct quotes from commanders, officials or public figures (e.g., Admiral Nimitz 'messaged a "Well done"', President Roosevelt quotes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting named officials or paraphrasing their messages provides authority and context. Identify the speaker and, where relevant, the office (e.g., 'Admiral Chester W. Nimitz, commander of the United States Pacific fleet').

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and background linking current actions to prior events
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide background that links the current report to earlier operations or developments (e.g., references to previous attacks, strengthened forces, or prior political events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brief contextual sentences (for example, 'as he did twelve days later after our second surprise attack...') help readers understand significance; include succinct historical linkage without digressing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational conditions and caveats affecting outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Report environmental or operational factors that influenced events (e.g., 'Foul weather and rain squalls forced our flyers to operate from dangerously low levels').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State weather, terrain, equipment limitations or other constraints that explain how and why events unfolded as reported; these caveats improve accuracy and nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest detail to illustrate conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use concrete, human-scale description of individuals' experiences and equipment to bring a scene to life (e.g., long description of soldiers' cold‑weather clothing and sleeping bags for Alaska duty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature sections like 'Consider Joe Doakes, private' with lists of clothing, boots, parkas, and everyday practice humanize abstract military facts—use sparingly to complement operational reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical and process detail for industrial reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: When covering production, industry or technology, include process steps and material/quantity specifics (e.g., steelmaking inputs and furnace temperatures, shipyard production plans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece provides detailed material balances and process descriptions; such technical specifics support claims about production capacity and effort—balance depth with readability for a general audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear sourcing and distinction of reports vs. broadcasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the origin of contested or foreign reports and distinguish them from confirmed official accounts (examples: 'The Berlin radio said', 'Domei said', 'Tokyo dispatch').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label potentially propagandistic or second‑hand reports and avoid presenting them as confirmed fact; where possible, note inability to directly protest or confirm (e.g., 'Actually, Japan is unable to lodge protests directly...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of subheads and segmented short items
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize a page with multiple short, titled items and occasional subheads to separate topics ('Forced Low By Weather', 'Troops Welcome Cold Weather, Glad to Get Out of Mud', 'Roosevelt Tells Of Hours').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This multi-item layout helps readers scan varied wartime coverage; use brief descriptive subheads that summarize the paragraph or block they introduce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of political/legislative context and quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting on government policy or law (e.g., manpower control, work-week debate, wartime wage policy), include quotes from principal actors and summarize proposed measures or positions (e.g., proposals for a nine‑member manpower committee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the proposals, who advocates them, and relevant arguments or evidence (Roosevelt on hours, Nelson/Kaiser testimony) so readers can evaluate policy significance.
